content.text: Oyster mushrooms are the easiest species to grow on a composted straw mix. They are fast-growing and tolerant of competition. But pasteurisation is still needed to knock back the main competing fungi. Shiitake on sawdust needs full sterilisation: it is slower to establish and cannot compete in unpasteurised substrate.
70 percent chopped straw: the primary food source.
15 percent mature garden compost: adds micronutrients and holds moisture in the block.
15 percent wood chip: slows degradation and provides structure.

Hot water pasteurisation: submerge the dry substrate mix in water at 70 to 80 degrees Celsius for 1 to 1.5 hours. Use a large pot or a clean plastic bin with boiling water poured over and weighted down. The compost thermometer confirms the temperature holds. After pasteurisation, spread the substrate on a clean surface to cool to below 28 degrees Celsius before inoculation.
is fastest when the substrate is inoculated warm but not hot.

Mix grain spawn into the cooled substrate at 10 to 15 percent by weight of the substrate. Mix thoroughly with clean hands or a clean tool. Pack into a clear plastic bag or a bucket with holes drilled at 100 mm intervals. The inoculated block should feel firm but not waterlogged: squeeze and a few drops of water should come out.

Place in a dark or low-light location at 18 to 24 degrees Celsius. Oyster mycelium colonises straw-compost substrate in 10 to 20 days. White growth visible through the bag confirms progress. If grey or green patches appear, contamination is present: the whole block must be discarded. When the block is fully white, move it to a fruiting environment: high humidity, some air exchange. And indirect light.

attrs.symptom: Green patches appearing in the block after 5 days

content.text: Green is Trichoderma mould, the main contaminant of straw-compost substrate. It indicates the pasteurisation was incomplete, the substrate was too wet. Or inoculation happened while the substrate was still too warm. Discard the block outdoors.
